title: The illustrated janamsakhi
hookLine: the B40 janamsakhi of 1733 comes with paintings of each sakhi

lines: A PICTURE BOOK ON A LAP.
POINT, AND THE STORY COMES BACK.
cards: A child on a parent's lap with a picture book, too young to read. They can't follow a word on the page, but they know the story anyway, because they know the pictures. Here's the wolf.
Here's the door. Point, and the story comes back. This week we've met janamsakhis as words: plain ones, warm ones, reflective ones.
Today, one that also speaks in pictures. It's known by a short, odd name: B40.

teach.b: B40 is a janamsakhi manuscript, and what sets it apart in this week's lessons is simple: its sakhis come with paintings. Turn a page and there's the story in words, and beside it, the same story in color.
Guru Nanak is there in scene after scene, and you learn to find him the way the child finds the wolf.

When his companion Mardana is there, look for the rabab, the stringed instrument the stories say he played while the Guru sang. Around them, the people of each story: holy men, kings, villagers, travelers.
The paintings don't try to show everything in the text.

They pick a moment, the meeting, the question, the turn, and hold it still. That's a choice, and a kind of reading: whoever painted a sakhi had to decide what the story was really about, and paint that.
Now think about who a book like this served. A page of writing speaks only to someone who can read it.
A painting speaks to anyone in the room. Gather round, point, and the story comes back, even for the child, even for the neighbor who never learned the script.
The pictures are tellers too, standing next to the words. And for us today, they're a window onto how Sikhs of their time imagined Guru Nanak: what he wore, how he sat, who was with him.
Not a photograph, but a picture of devotion.

how: Paintings of sakhis from manuscripts such as the B40 janamsakhi are reproduced in books and exhibitions, and Sikh families and teachers use illustrated sakhis to tell Guru Nanak's stories to children.

a painted portrait of the ten Gurus
a collection of Guru Nanak's life-stories

games.why: the paintings in B40 pick a moment, the meeting, the question, the turn, and hold it still.

practice: Look slowly at an old painting, one of Guru Nanak from an old manuscript or any old painting at all, or, if none is at hand, picture a scene from a sakhi you know.

Find the main figure, then the people around him, then let your eyes go to the corners and the hands, and ask which moment the painter chose, and why that one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end.
